sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: As tasks and environments change after deployment, agents need mechanisms for continued adaptation. Harness self-evolution uses execution feedback to revise instructions, memory, and control logic while keeping model weights fixed. Later runs load accepted revisions, and the update mechanism remains available to learn from subsequent experience (Section 2). This process builds on recursive self-improvement and self-referential problem solving in the context of contemporary agents (Good, 1965; Schmidhuber, 2003). Adaptation can revise model weights or the harness governing prompts, memory, workflows, and tools. Our focus on the latter rests on three considerations. First, the harness directly shapes fixed models behavior, while reusable procedures preserve task constraints and lessons from earlier failures (Chan et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Second, harness revisions reuse an existing model deployment, avoiding retraining and additional weight checkpoints. This can reduce adaptation and maintenance costs and permits updates through proprietary APIs without access to model weights. Third, instructions, memory records, and code support direct inspection, version comparison, and change tracking; attributing behavioral differences between model checkpoints can require additional controlled experiments. We hold the task model fixed to isolate harness selfevolution, with joint modelharness evolution addressed in Section 6.1. Existing methods vary in what is modified, how candidates are generated, and how revisions are admitted (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Robeyns et al., 2025). We first classify the update target: the state modified and inherited by later runs. Interpreted-state updates revise instructions, stored experience, or task-level coordination over predefined capabilities; executable revisions change capability implementations, runtime control logic, or plugin-based service composition (Section 3; Figure 1). Empirical selection alone does not establish generalization or retention. Section 4 relates candidate search to evolutionary structures, then uses stability and concentration results to state conditions for expected generalization, bounded accumulated regressions, and high-probability admission. Persistent state also determines how revisions propagate and which consequences software recovery can address, motivating system design choices, continual validation, and independent safety controls (Sections 56). This work makes three contributions: Definition and Operational Taxonomy (Sections 23). We define persistent feedback-driven lifecycle and organize interpreted-state updates and executable revisions by their mutation boundaries. Conditional Theoretical Analysis (Section 4). We map harness search to evolutionary structures and derive conditions for expected generalization, bounded accumulated regressions, and highprobability admission from classical stability and concentration results. Systems Implications and Design Trade-offs (Sections 56). We analyze propagation and repair burdens in five settings and connect attributed cases (Sections 3 and 6) to modelharness pairing, deployment, and reuse decisions, with continual validation and safety constraints. Associated resources are available at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

It may draw on historical feedback, archived candidates, and additional validation rollouts. If no revision is admitted, the incumbent is retained: Hk = Hk1. Each retained revision changes the state used for subsequent execution, whose feedback can guide the next update. This lifecycle requires: 1. Operational feedback and update continuity. The system uses feedback from its own executions to construct or select revisions algorithmically, and retains the mechanism for further updates. Environments, automated assessors, and people may provide feedback; admission may require human approval. 2. Persistence across runs. Accepted revisions are stored and loaded in subsequent run, allowing experience from one interaction to influence later execution. These requirements concern repeatability: one observed update can demonstrate the capability if both hold. Appending logs or compacting context under fixed rules does not revise the harness; learning reusable procedures or changing memory policies can. Revising the update mechanism adds another level of recursion. Self-evolution denotes the update process; self-improvement denotes Scope and terminology. gain established by comparison. We use harness RSI (recursive self-improvement) as the name of the research area, without assuming that each revision helps. Weight-only adaptation and scaffolds without an update mechanism fall outside this scope. When system also trains weights, we examine its harness updates with the task model held fixed.

sections.title: 3 THE TAXONOMY OF HARNESS SELF-EVOLUTION
sections.content: EURISKOs heuristic revision and the Gödel Machines proof-governed self-rewriting established distinct antecedents of harness self-evolution (Lenat, 1983; Schmidhuber, 2003). Contemporary methods use empirical feedback to revise prompts, consolidate persistent memory, and search workflow specifications around fixed model (Agrawal et al., 2026; Fernando et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025b). The interpreted/executable distinction concerns the edited artifacts role, not its programming language. Workflow revisions remain interpreted when they change task-level sequencing or routing through fixed coordination interfaces over predefined 3 Self-evolving Agent Harness Preprint operators. This includes code that only composes those operators; revising operator implementations or the runtime mechanisms that enact coordination constitutes an executable revision, even under an unchanged executor. We organize executable targets into component implementations, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. The first two describe mutation scope; the third describes how components and runtime services are bound and replaced. Plugin composition can span component implementations and repository-level logic, so revision may belong to more than one category. Classifying the update target does not determine whether method satisfies the feedback, continuity, and persistence requirements in Section 2. 3.1 TOOLS AND CODE PATCHES Component-level revision confines mutation to callable procedures or designated modules while keeping surrounding orchestration outside the editable surface. Where entry points and I/O contracts remain fixed, candidates replace component implementations; tool synthesis may instead extend the callable interface. Skill libraries retain executable functions for later retrieval and composition (Wang et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025); patch-based architectures, including Self-Harness, HarnessCompass, and Agentic Harness Engineering, constrain trace-guided mutation to selected components (Zhang et al., 2026a;d; Lin et al., 2026). Editing memory-management functions changes the harness machinery, whereas curating stored entries changes its interpreted state (Zhang et al., 2025a). Within this boundary, candidate archives preserve alternatives for subsequent search (Luo et al., 2026), while protocol perturbations test whether an evolved harnesss gain over the initial harness survives changes in assessment conditions (Zhu et al., 2026). Stable interfaces facilitate replacement and local checks, but changed outputs or shared state can propagate regressions beyond the edited module. 3.2 REPOSITORY AND RUNTIME LOGIC Repository-level search exposes context construction, orchestration loops, execution hooks, recovery, and termination to revision. The boundary concerns control over interactions among harness components, rather than the number of files edited. Whole-agent synthesis searches complete control programs, while repository evolution retains implementation lineages for later selection and revision (Hu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026b; Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b;g; Wang et al., 2025a). Changes to shared context, scheduling, or recovery can alter the inputs and execution assumptions of otherwise unchanged components. This coupling motivates edit constraints, transferoriented admission, and deployment checks (Xia et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026a). Archive membership preserves candidate for further search; adoption additionally requires promoting the selected program into the runtime used by later tasks. Extending mutation to the optimizers prompts, hooks, and tools makes the update mechanism itself evolvable (Wang et al., 2026). An exported program satisfies the continuing lifecycle only if its deployment retains an update mechanism. HarnessOpt extends the SkillOpt-Lite study from skill editing to runtime revision, improving spreadsheet previews, output checks, and recovery after tool failures (Shen et al., 2026a). On SpreadsheetBench  (Table 2)  , GPT-5.4-nano with HarnessOpt and skill reaches 77.58%, exceeding GPT-5.5 with SkillOpt (76.20%); across all four models, HarnessOpt with skill improves on SkillOpt-Lite by 5.6911.39 percentage points. This crossover illustrates modelharness pairing, but does not establish superiority at matched cost. Table 2: SpreadsheetBench accuracy (%), converted from proportions in Table 3 of Shen et al. The editable object may be component implementation or binding that determines which implementation supplies runtime service, such as memory storage, tool dispatch, or the agent loop. Composition here therefore reaches beyond task-level routing among fixed operators. Kernel-defined substrates specify how these services are connected, mounted, and replaced (DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Shi et al., 2026); feedback-driven systems revise typed primitives, versioned resources, or scoped modules under interface and validation constraints (Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026f; Wu et al., 2026a). This organization can expose both local capabilities and core runtime services while retaining explicit constraints on their composition. Everything Is Plugin (EIP) extends it to capabilities generated, validated, and mounted during operation. Interface contracts support compatibility checks and component replacement; they do not establish behavioral isolation or safe admission. Adoption still requires validation of the composed behavior. Using DSH Everything, Codex plugin lets the agent generate tools during execution and retain them for later tasks (Shen, 2026; Pan, 2026). In simulated office workload, spreadsheets from different company regions vary in language and content but share similar calculations. sections.title: 4 THEORY OF HARNESS SELF-EVOLUTION
sections.content: Many harness optimizers explore discrete instructions, skills, and code through execution-guided proposals rather than gradients through the edits. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) characterize the search structure; continual-learning analysis relates empirical gains to generalization and capability retention. Recent work likewise distinguishes optimization from generalization and links reliable adoption to verification cost (Gan et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026b). 4.1 AN EVOLUTIONARY PERSPECTIVE ON HARNESS SEARCH The EA view separates four aspects of an update: the representation of mutable state, the variation that generates edits, the assessment of their fitness, and the selection of state to retain. Traces and critiques can guide variation, while admission depends on the resulting assessment. Local elitism concentrates search around an incumbent; archive-based diversity preserves alternative lineages; Pareto selection balances competing objectives. Figure 2 summarizes eight algorithmic correspondences, their limits, and representative methods. Because all three mechanisms select on empirical fitness, accepted revisions can overfit or forget, motivating the generalization and retention analysis below. 4.2 GENERALIZATION AND RETENTION FROM CONTINUAL PAC-LEARNING PERSPECTIVE Lasting capability requires controls on generalization, forgetting, and admission uncertainty. sections.title: 5 APPLICATIONS AND SOCIETAL IMPACTS
sections.content: Persistent harness revisions preserve learned procedures across tasks. We examine their implications for knowledge sharing, reliability, and accountability in five application settings. Personal workspaces. Revisable instructions, memory, and skills preserve project conventions and user preferences across programming, writing, and research sessions (Anthropic, 2026; GitHub, 2026; Anthropic, 2025). Playbook revision and trajectory distillation convert execution feedback into reusable procedures that can reduce repeated setup and diagnosis (Zhang et al., 2026e; Ni et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026a). As updates accumulate, users may struggle to track changes: temporary workarounds become standing rules, and injected instructions persist across tasks (Gadgil et al., 2026). Even successful task executions can yield skills that generalize harmfully (Zhang et al., 2026c). Reviewable changes and artifact provenance support ongoing curation; recovery must encompass derived skills, memory, and caches as well as tracked code. Enterprise automation. Shared skill libraries and revisable agent components let teams reuse incident diagnoses, API adaptations, and recovery procedures as operational requirements change (Ma et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026g; Lin et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026a). Local workarounds can spread to teams with different permission or data assumptions. Shared faulty procedures may cause correlated errors that escape detection, extending concerns about algorithmic monoculture to persistent harness artifacts (Kleinberg & Raghavan, 2021; Bommasani et al., 2022). Remediation requires identifying consumers, withdrawing affected versions, restoring dependent workflows, and investigating unauthorized actions. Version-linked deployment records and staged rollout support containment, while service disruption or data exposure may require organizational redress after software recovery. Scientific discovery. Persistent settings, failure reports, and search heuristics help collaborators reuse earlier trials (Qu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). Diagnostic evaluations also document failures to check claims against evidence and artifacts (Fei et al., 2026). When evolving protocols exploit provisional checks or imperfect external metrics, specification gaming can reinforce procedures that fail independent measurement (Skalse et al., 2022; Baker et al., 2025). These procedures can spread through collaboration or wet-lab transfer, consuming instrument time, reagents, and expert effort before detection. Final assessment must remain outside the editable surface (Section 2); independent measurement and replication are also needed to establish scientific validity. Robotics and embodied interaction. EMHO revises planning, observation handling, and recovery around frozen model (Lee et al., 2026a); RoboRSI revises and reuses hierarchy of robot skills (Wen et al., 2026). Memory Transfer Planning adapts code from fixed memory, including transfer from simulation to hardware (Kagaya et al., 2025); EmbodiedSWE learns weights from verified simulation trajectories (Shen et al., 2026b). Errors in accepted action code can persist across motions, causing excessive force, unsafe recovery, or incorrect contact behavior. Software rollback changes future commands but cannot reverse deformation, wear, or injury. For physical deployment, we recommend keeping emergency stops, force and speed limits, and authorization checks outside the editable surface, with independent action checks and staged trials. Revision-linked command records support investigation and remediation. Self-evolving Agent Harness Preprint Public services and clinical systems. Revisable triage, eligibility routing, and case-processing procedures offer an inspectable way to incorporate changing guidelines and operational feedback; current evidence includes prototype clinical interactions and context adaptation on diagnostic and legal tasks (Jiang et al., 2025; Schmidgall et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026). Qualified professionals must validate and authorize consequential revisions. Erroneous preferences can otherwise become persistent rules that reproduce institutional disadvantage across cases (Citron, 2008; Shao et al., 2026). Patients and applicants may lack access to an alternative institution. Software rollback cannot recover missed treatment window or, by itself, correct denied entitlements and corrupted records. Execution-log inspection aids agent evaluation (Kapoor et al., 2026). For accountability, we recommend recording each decisions rule version, evidence, and admission history, alongside accessible review, appeal, and remediation.

sections.title: 6 FUTURE DIRECTIONS
sections.content: The executable-revision cases in Section 3 motivate research on modelharness co-design and plugin lifecycles. We also examine distributed execution, continual validation, and safety boundaries for evolving systems. 6.1 MODELHARNESS CO-DESIGN The modelharness crossover in Section 3.2 motivates studying how to allocate adaptation effort between the model and its runtime. Budget-matched studies should compare model selection, skill optimization, runtime revision, and weight updates (Chen et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b), accounting for both adaptation and subsequent execution costs. Testing frozen, transferred, and re-evolved harnesses across checkpoints would distinguish transferable gains from those requiring further harness evolution. Joint adaptation should also examine which update order preserves earlier capabilities as model behavior and runtime assumptions change. 6.2 DISTRIBUTED EXECUTION AND EDGE INFRASTRUCTURE Runtime revision (Section 3.2) can change both execution cost and where components are best placed. fixed-deployment study illustrates the communication trade-offs: Shen et al. (2023) compare Jetson Nano client, an RTX 4090 edge server, and Azure under workload of 10% classification, 40% captioning, and 50% visual question answering. Clientedge execution partitions expert networks and compresses task-relevant features; the edge-only baseline transmits losslessly compressed input images. Clientedge co-inference minimizes latency across 100500 KB/s in this study (Figure 3). Future studies should include harness synthesis, validation, and distribution costs when comparing deployment choices across network conditions and update frequencies, at matched quality and subject to privacy constraints. Figure 3: Latency adapted from Shen et al. (2023); clientedge in green. 9 Self-evolving Agent Harness Preprint 6.3 PLUGIN CREATION AND REUSE The creation overhead and subsequent savings in Section 3.3 motivate lifecycle-aware decisions about when to reuse, revalidate, regenerate, or retire plugin. Future studies should measure the number of related tasks needed to recover generation and validation costs at matched quality, including repair and dependency-maintenance costs. Varying task similarity, reuse frequency, and interface changes would reveal when retained tool remains useful and when regeneration is preferable. Admission should test the resulting composition, since locally valid plugin can alter shared state or the behavior of other components. 6.4 CONTINUAL VALIDATION UNDER DISTRIBUTION AND EVALUATOR DRIFT Time-stamped tasks (White et al., 2024; Jain et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2026), version-pinned environments (Merrill et al., 2026), and difficulty calibration (Chen et al., 2026c) help distinguish harness gains from workload drift. Admission requires fresh independent tasks (Section 4.2); adaptive reuse needs separate statistical controls (Dwork et al., 2015b; Blum & Hardt, 2015). Reused calibration tasks cannot replace fresh admission evidence. Judge bias (Lù et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024) requires independent calibration of η in Equation (9) after evaluator changes. Protecting does not prevent specification gaming (Pan et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2026). Allocating budgets among calibration, admission, and regression checks remains an open problem. 6.5 SAFETY BOUNDARIES FOR SELF-MODIFYING SYSTEMS External safeguards complement model alignment (Bai et al., 2022). Context-removal and transfer tests can probe harmful skill generalization (Zhang et al., 2026c; Wu et al., 2026b); data-flow and tool-sequence constraints support runtime enforcement (Doshi et al., 2026). We recommend least privilege, time-limited grants, and isolation; creating capabilities must not confer authority. Rollback covers only effects within its recovery model (Shi et al., 2026), motivating authorization and physical or spending limits for consequential actions. Validating composed behavior and revoking grants as dependencies change remain open problems. Defenses should be evaluated by attack success, isolation time, and legitimate-work overhead.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Our framework defines harness self-evolution through feedback-driven revision, continuing update It separates mutation boundaries from search capability, and persistence around fixed models. and admission, distinguishing expected generalization, budget-constrained retention, and highprobability acceptance under fresh validation. Persistent revisions preserve knowledge but can spread errors with irreversible consequences. Their deployment requires continual validation under distribution and evaluator drift, with independent controls over learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. 10 Self-evolving Agent Harness Preprint

sections.title: A EXTENDED TECHNICAL REPORT
sections.content: This paper presents self-contained framework for harness self-evolution. For broader literature coverage and extended discussions of evaluation, applications, and societal implications, see our companion technical report, Harness Self-Evolution: Theory, Algorithms, Evaluation, Applications, and Impact, at https://openreview.net/pdf?id=m5jsFGXUM2. Contents of the companion report. 1. Introduction 2. Definition of Harness Self-Evolution 3. Interpreted Update Targets 3.1 From Recursive Self-Improvement to Harness Adaptation 3.2 Instructions and Prompts 3.3 Context, Memory, and Reusable Procedures 3.4 Agentic Workflows and Topologies 4. Executable Update Targets 4.1 Tools and Code Patches 4.2 Repository and Runtime Logic 4.3 Everything Is Plugin 5. Theory of Harness Self-Evolution 5.1 An Evolutionary Perspective on Harness Search 5.2 Generalization and Retention from Continual PAC-Learning Perspective 6. Evaluating Harness Self-Evolution 6.1 Four Claims Behind Task Score 6.2 Current Evaluation Practices and Benchmarks 6.3 Longitudinal and Dynamic Evaluation 7. Applications of Harness Self-Evolution 7.1 Personal Assistance and Developer Workspaces 7.2 Enterprise Automation 7.3 Scientific Discovery 7.4 Robotics and Embodied Interaction 7.5 Public Services and Clinical Systems 8. Societal and Economic Implications 8.1 Productivity, Work, and Education 8.2 Economic Distribution and Market Structure 8.3 Innovation and Public-Service Capacity 8.4 Privacy, Security, and Systemic Stability 8.5 Governance and Institutional Power 9. Future Directions 9.1 ModelHarness Co-Evolution 9.2 Optimization Algorithms for Heterogeneous Harness Search 9.3 Infrastructure for Evolving State 9.4 Dynamic Evaluation and Benchmark Refresh 9.5 Safety Boundaries for Self-Modifying Systems 9.6 Governance, Provenance, and Human Oversight 10. Conclusion
